---
title: "Quiz: non-rigid registration"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

---

**Q1.** Why is optical flow not enough to align a live-cell image with an immunostaining of the same sample made after fixation?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which two assumptions of optical flow fail?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Brightness constancy fails (different stains, different contrast) and the motion need not be small (fixation and mounting deform the sample by many pixels). Registration instead optimises a similarity measure that tolerates contrast changes, over a smooth family of deformations, starting from a rigid alignment.
:::

---

**Q2.** In a B-spline free-form deformation with control points every 16 px, you move one control point by 9 px. Which pixels move, and by how much does the pixel at that control point move?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Each control point is a bump 4 spacings wide; the bump is 4/6 at its centre in each direction.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Only pixels within 2 spacings (32 px) in $x$ and in $y$ move: a 64 × 64 px patch. The pixel at the control point moves $9 \cdot \tfrac46 \cdot \tfrac46 = 4$ px; at the next control point along a row, $9 \cdot \tfrac16 \cdot \tfrac46 = 1$ px; diagonally, $9/36 = 0.25$ px.
:::

---

**Q3.** The Jacobian determinant of a registration result is 0.6 in one region, 1.8 in another and −0.2 in a third. Interpret each.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
It is the local change of area.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
0.6: the region is smaller in the moving image than in the fixed one (compressed to 60 % of its area). 1.8: larger (expanded by 80 %). −0.2: folding, the map turns space inside out; physically impossible, a sign of too little regularisation (or a wrong optimum).
:::

---

**Q4.** Which similarity measure would you use for (a) two frames of a brightfield time-lapse, (b) a DAPI image and a brightfield image of the same cells, (c) an H&E section and an immunofluorescence section?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How are the grey values of the two images related?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
(a) SSD (or NCC if the illumination drifts): same contrast. (b) Mutual information: the relation between the two contrasts is consistent but not a straight line (nuclei bright in DAPI, grey or dark in brightfield). (c) Mutual information (after converting H&E to one channel, e.g. haematoxylin): two stains, any consistent relation.
:::

---

**Q5.** Two images are exact inverses of each other ($B = 255 - A$). What are their NCC and MI? Why does SSD fail to align them?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Does knowing $A$ tell you $B$?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
NCC = −1 (a perfect straight-line relation with negative slope). MI is maximal: $\mathrm{MI} = H(A) = H(B)$, because $B$ is determined by $A$. SSD is largest exactly at the true alignment (bright on dark everywhere), so minimising SSD moves away from it.
:::

---

**Q6.** A registration with a very fine control grid and no bending penalty gives a perfect match, but the Jacobian map shows a strong blob of shrinkage where a tumour grew between two time points. What went wrong?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What is the deformation allowed to explain?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The deformation was free enough to "explain away" a real change (growth) as a deformation. A perfect match is not a correct result. Use a coarser grid or a bending penalty, look at the Jacobian map critically, and check with held-out landmarks.
:::

---

**Q7.** *(math)* Show that $\mathrm{MI} = H(A) + H(B) - H(A, B)$ equals $\sum_{a,b}p(a,b)\log_2\frac{p(a,b)}{p(a)p(b)}$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Write $H(A) = -\sum_{a,b}p(a,b)\log_2 p(a)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Since $p(a) = \sum_b p(a,b)$: $H(A) = -\sum_{a,b}p(a,b)\log_2 p(a)$ and $H(B) = -\sum_{a,b}p(a,b)\log_2 p(b)$. Then $H(A) + H(B) - H(A,B) = \sum_{a,b}p(a,b)\big[\log_2 p(a,b) - \log_2 p(a) - \log_2 p(b)\big] = \sum_{a,b}p(a,b)\log_2\frac{p(a,b)}{p(a)p(b)}$.
:::
